facts.statement: Panoplosaurus was named by Lawrence Lambe in 1919.
facts.quote: parent_authority: Lambe, 1919

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus lived during the middle Campanian stage, roughly 76 to 75 million years ago.
facts.quote: Few specimens of the genus are known, all from the middle Campanian of the Dinosaur Park Formation, roughly 76 to 75 million years ago.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus was first discovered in 1917 and named in 1919 by Lawrence Lambe, with the name meaning "well-armoured lizard".
facts.quote: It was first discovered in 1917, and named in 1919 by Lawrence Lambe, named for its extensive armour, meaning "well-armoured lizard".

facts.statement: Charles M. Sternberg discovered the holotype of Panoplosaurus in 1917 in Quarry 69 of the Belly River Group, 210 feet above sea level.
facts.quote: In 1917, Canadian paleontologist Charles M. Sternberg of the Geological Survey of Canada discovered a complete skull and significant amount of the skeleton of an armoured dinosaur in the sandstone layers of Quarry 69 of the Belly River Group, 210 ft above sea level.

facts.statement: A scapula from the Kirtland Formation in New Mexico was referred to Panoplosaurus in 1981, but it may instead belong to Nodocephalosaurus due to age and location differences, though this remains uncertain.
facts.quote: A scapula from the Naashoibito member of the Kirtland Formation in New Mexico was referred to Panoplosaurus in 1981, but as it is from a different age and location from other specimens, may instead represent the ankylosaurid taxon Nodocephalosaurus, although this is uncertain due to lack of overlapping material.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus is a genus of armoured dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus is a genus of armoured dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, Canada.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus was a quadrupedal animal roughly 5 meters long and weighing 1600 kilograms.
facts.quote: It was a quadrupedal animal, roughly 5 m long and 1600 kg in weight.

facts.statement: A prominent armour plate covering the cheek is present in the type specimen of Panoplosaurus, which may be a unique feature of the taxon or just the individual.
facts.quote: There is also a prominent armour plate covering the cheek in the type specimen of Panoplosaurus, which may be unique feature of the taxon, or individual, depending on what additional skulls are referred to P. mirus.

facts.statement: The skull of Panoplosaurus is broad and depressed, forming a triangular shape at the end of its blunt snout.
facts.quote: The skull of Panoplosaurus is broad and depressed, narrowing towards the end of the blunt snout to form a triangular shape.

facts.statement: The skull of Panoplosaurus measures 335 mm in straight-line length but 530 mm across the curved skull roof.
facts.quote: At a total length of 335 mm in a straight line, the skull is curved in a way that across the skull roof the same length is 530 mm.

facts.statement: The skull of Panoplosaurus reaches a maximum width of 295 mm behind the orbits, giving it a short and broad appearance.
facts.quote: Behind the orbits, the skull reaches its maximum width of 295 mm, giving it a very short and broad appearance.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus had very small orbits placed far from a squared snout that featured laterally open nostrils.
facts.quote: The orbits of Panoplosaurus are very small, and placed far from the snout, which is very squared and bearing laterally open nostrils.

facts.statement: Bony plates covered the entire exterior of the Panoplosaurus skull, including large osteoderms on the sides and mandible, small scutes in the nostrils, and small ossicles underneath the head.
facts.quote: Bony plates are present across the entire exterior of the skull, including large osteoderms on all the sides of the skull and mandible, small scutes within the nostrils, and underneath the head in the form of an aggregation of small ossicles covering the surface between the two lower jaws.

facts.statement: The occipital of Panoplosaurus faced nearly directly downwards, suggesting the animal held its head with the snout about 20 degrees below the horizontal.
facts.quote: The occipital, where the skull articulates with the neck, is short and thick, facing nearly directly downwards, which would have meant the head was held with the snout down in life, about 20 degrees below the horizontal.

facts.statement: Unlike Edmontonia, the groove separating cranial osteoderms never disappeared in Panoplosaurus, indicating a unique narrow scute across the rear of the skull.
facts.quote: Unlike in Edmontonia, the groove separating cranial osteoderms in Panoplosaurus never disappear, which show that there is a unique narrow scute across the entire rear of the skull.

facts.statement: Due to fusion and osteoderm coverage, only the predentary bone of the 310 mm long Panoplosaurus mandible could be identified.
facts.quote: Due to fusion and the covering of osteoderms, the only individual bone of the 310 mm long mandible than can be identified is the predentary.

facts.statement: The horseshoe-shaped predentaries of Panoplosaurus formed a sharp beak that fit within the overhang of the upper jaw premaxillaries.
facts.quote: Predentaries, which make up the lower portion of the snout, are somewhat horseshoe-shaped, form a sharp beak that fits within the overhang of the premaxillaries in the upper jaw.

facts.statement: Both the predentaries and premaxillaries of Panoplosaurus lacked teeth, a derived feature among nodosaurids.
facts.quote: Both the predentaries and their premaxillary counterparts lack any teeth, a derived feature among nodosaurids where premaxillary teeth are sometimes present.

facts.statement: Eight maxillary teeth were preserved in Panoplosaurus, though the total count may have been higher, the jaw had limited space for additional teeth.
facts.quote: Eight maxillary teeth are preserved, and though it is not certain that was the full tooth count there is not room for many more in the jaw.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus teeth resembled those of Edmontonia and Palaeoscincus, featuring a mild crown expansion above the root and denticles with more ridges on the front edge than the rear.
facts.quote: All the teeth are similar to those of Edmontonia and Palaeoscincus, with a mild expansion of the crown above the root (cingulum), and denticles formed by prominent ridges on both the front and rear edges of the crown, though there are more on the front than rear edge of the tooth.

facts.statement: The first three cervical vertebrae after the skull were fused into a single ossification in Panoplosaurus, a feature unique to it and Edmontonia among ankylosaurs.
facts.quote: The first three cervicals after the skull are fused together into one single ossification, a feature unique to Panoplosaurus and Edmontonia among ankylosaurs.

facts.statement: The scapula and coracoid were completely fused in Panoplosaurus, with only a slight thickening indicating the original suture.
facts.quote: The scapula and coracoid are completely fused together, with the only indication of the bone separation being a slight thickening along what would be the suture.

facts.statement: The scapula of Panoplosaurus was 410 mm long and the coracoid was 255 mm long.
facts.quote: The scapula itself is 410 mm long, and the coracoid is 255 mm.

facts.statement: The robust humerus of Panoplosaurus was 430 mm long, suggesting its upper arm was held in a flexed position during life.
facts.quote: The humerus is a robust, 430 mm long bone, with the shape and projection of the head suggesting the upper arm of Panoplosaurus was held in a flexed position in life.

facts.statement: All ungual bones of Panoplosaurus were hoof-shaped, lacking a point and having a flat bottom.
facts.quote: All ungual bones were hoof-shaped, lacking a point and bearing a flat bottom.

facts.statement: The articulated tibia and fibula of Panoplosaurus measured 385 mm and 310 mm respectively, with the tibia being noticeably longer.
facts.quote: The right tibia and fibula were found still in articulation, with the 385 mm tibia being noticeably longer than the 310 mm fibula.

facts.statement: The first category of osteoderms in Panoplosaurus consisted of large, paired elements with a low keel that formed bands around the neck from the head.
facts.quote: The first kind was large, paired elements with a low keel, which formed bands around the neck leading from the head.

facts.statement: The second category of osteoderms in Panoplosaurus were slightly smaller, suboval individual elements with a strong keel located from the sides of the neck to the back.
facts.quote: On the sides of the neck to the back was a second kind, individual elements that were slightly smaller, suboval, and had a strong keel.

facts.statement: Small, keeled scutes with a thick base formed the fourth osteoderm type in Panoplosaurus, occurring on the underside of the neck base extending to the chin.
facts.quote: Small, keeled scutes with a thick base were identified as the fourth osteoderm type, occurring on the underside of the base of the neck forwards to the chin.

facts.statement: Carpenter questioned the identification of four sacrals in Panoplosaurus in 1990, noting that Edmontonia has only three true sacrals, though he could not definitively identify the first sacral as a dorsosacral.
facts.quote: The identification of four sacrals was questioned by Carpenter in 1990, as Edmontonia only has three true sacrals, but he was not able to definitively identify the first sacral of Sternberg as a dorsosacral.

facts.statement: Lambe named the genus Panoplosaurus in 1919.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus was originally named simply as a genus of armoured dinosaur by Lambe in 1919

facts.statement: Sternberg classified Panoplosaurus within the family Ankylosauridae in 1921.
facts.quote: though it was subsequently specified by Sternberg in 1921 that within Stegosauria it was closest to taxa like Ankylosaurus and Euoplocephalus, and so within Ankylosauridae

facts.statement: Sternberg described Edmontonia as a very close relative of Panoplosaurus in 1928.
facts.quote: The description of the new genus Edmontonia in 1928 by Sternberg identified it as a very close relative of Panoplosaurus

facts.statement: Franz Nopcsa proposed a new classification for Panoplosaurus in 1929 after describing Struthiosaurus.
facts.quote: Following further description of the armoured taxon Struthiosaurus by Franz Nopcsa in 1929, a different classification war proposed

facts.statement: Charles W. Gilmore amended Nopcsa's classification of Panoplosaurinae in 1930.
facts.quote: Nopcsa's classification of Panoplosaurinae was amended slightly by Charles W. Gilmore in 1930

facts.statement: Loris S. Russell placed Panoplosaurus in the subfamily Edmontoniinae in 1940.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus was then placed in the new subfamily Edmontoniinae by Loris S. Russell in 1940

facts.statement: Evgeny Maleev classified Panoplosaurus in the family Ankylosauridae.
facts.quote: Evgeny Maleev moved Panoplosaurus into the family Ankylosauridae

facts.statement: Coombs revised the classification of Ankylosauria in 1978.
facts.quote: Coombs reviewed and revised the classifications of Ankylosauria in 1978

facts.statement: Paul Sereno revived the subfamily Panoplosaurinae in 1986.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurinae was then revived in 1986 by Paul Sereno

facts.statement: Robert Bakker redescribed Late Cretaceous North American nodosaurid specimens in 1988.
facts.quote: Robert Bakker then redescribed specimens from the Late Cretaceous of North America in 1988

facts.statement: Carpenter reviewed Late Cretaceous North American nodosaurids in 1990.
facts.quote: Carpenter further reviewed Late Cretaceous North American nodosaurids in 1990

facts.statement: Sereno modified his classification of Panoplosaurus in 1998.
facts.quote: In 1998, Sereno modified his earlier position, using the name Nodosaurinae for the group of derived nodosaurids including Panoplosaurus

facts.statement: Tracy Ford published a new classification of Panoplosaurus in 2000.
facts.quote: Tracy Ford published a novel classification of Panoplosaurus in 2000

facts.statement: Yuong-Nam Lee conducted the first phylogenetic analysis including Panoplosaurus in 1996.
facts.quote: The first phylogenetic analysis to include Panoplosaurus was that of Yuong-Nam Lee in 1996

facts.statement: Carpenter's 2001 analysis placed Panoplosaurus next to a clade of Sauropelta and Silvisaurus.
facts.quote: the 2001 analysis of Carpenter instead recovered Edmontonia closest to Animantarx, while Panoplosaurus nested next to a clade of Sauropelta and Silvisaurus

facts.statement: Hill and colleagues' 2003 analysis resolved Panoplosaurus as the sister taxon to a group of Edmontonia and Animantarx.
facts.quote: The 2003 analysis of Robert Hill and colleagues resolved a group of Edmontonia and Animantarx, with Panoplosaurus as the sister taxon

facts.statement: Thompson and colleagues combined ankylosaurian analyses in 2012.
facts.quote: Richard Thompson and colleagues in 2012, combining previous ankylosaurian analyses into a single one to analyse both Nodosauridae and Ankylosauridae

facts.statement: Arbour and Currie expanded a phylogenetic analysis in 2016 to include many nodosaurids.
facts.quote: In 2016, the phylogenetic analysis of Arbour and Currie initially meant to test the relationships of Ankylosauridae was expanded to include many of the nodosaurids known at the time

facts.statement: Madzia and colleagues named the clade uniting Panoplosaurus and related taxa Panoplosaurini.
facts.quote: Daniel Madzia and colleagues decided to name the clade uniting all taxa closer to Panoplosaurus than Nodosaurus or Struthiosaurus, giving it the formal name Panoplosaurini

facts.statement: Soto Acuña and colleagues modified the Panoplosaurus phylogeny in 2021 and 2024.
facts.quote: Additional modifications to the analysis were done by Soto Acuña and colleagues in 2021 and 2024

facts.statement: The variability of Panoplosaurus teeth implies a less restrictive feeding strategy than a simple soft-food diet.
facts.quote: While the shape of teeth in Panoplosaurus and other ankylosaurs suggests a simple, soft food diet, their variability implies a less restrictive feeding strategy

facts.statement: Microwear on Panoplosaurus teeth indicates a diet of abundant foliage with occasional fruit.
facts.quote: microwear on the teeth of ankylosaurids and Panoplosaurus instead show that their diets were not significantly different, with regular pitting and abrasion showing a diet consisting occasionally of fruit as well as more abundant foliage

facts.statement: The presence of gastroliths in Panoplosaurus is uncertain because they were not found in the original specimen material.
facts.quote: Gastroliths may have been found with Panoplosaurus as well, but their identification is uncertain as they were not originally mentioned among the material found as part of the specimen

facts.statement: The nasal passage of Panoplosaurus loops 360 degrees twice in different planes before reaching the olfactory recess.
facts.quote: The complete nasal passage of Panoplosaurus undergoes two complete 360 degree loops in different planes along its length, before entering the olfactory recess for scent processing.

facts.statement: Simulations suggest air passing through Panoplosaurus's nasal passages warmed by 17.9 to 18.2 degrees Celsius and became saturated with moisture.
facts.quote: Inflowing air in Panoplosaurus was simulated to undergo a raise of between 17.9 and 18.2 C, primarily in the elongate nasal passage, while saturating the air with moisture.

facts.statement: The brain of Panoplosaurus occupies 33% of the skull's length, which is higher than in other ankylosaurids.
facts.quote: The brain of Panoplosaurus takes up 33% of the length of the skull, similar to the nodosaurid Pawpawsaurus where the value is 30%, a higher value than in ankylosaurids.

facts.statement: The ground in the Panoplosaurus habitat was covered with mosses, lichens, fungi, and decaying plant matter.
facts.quote: The ground would have been covered with mosses, lichens, and fungi, and a layer of decaying plant matter.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus mirus is the only known species of the extinct nodosaurid dinosaur Panoplosaurus, which lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 79 to 73 million years ago, in what is now North America.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus mirus es la única especie conocida del género extinto Panoplosaurus (gr. "lagarto completamente armado") de dinosaurio tireóforo nodosáurido, que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente entre 79 y 73 millones de años, en el Campaniense, en lo que es hoy Norteamérica.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus was a compact dinosaur measuring 5 to 7 meters in length, 2 meters in height, and weighing approximately 1.5 to 1.6 tons.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus fue un dinosaurio de constitución compacta de entre 5 a 7 metros de largo y 2 de alto, llegando a pesar cerca de 1,5 a 1,6 toneladas de peso.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus's heavy armor consisted of sharp spines along the sides of the neck, shoulders, and sides of the thorax and belly.
facts.quote: Su pesada armadura estaba compuesta por espinas afiladas a los lados del cuello, hombros y costados del tórax y vientre.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus had a narrow head with spines over the eyes and a mouth with blade-like teeth for stripping plants, connected to the body by a short neck protected by square plates.
facts.quote: La cabeza era angosta con púas sobre los ojos y con una boca con dientes como laminas para desgajar las plantas, que se unía al cuerpo por un corto cuello protegido por placas cuadradas.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus likely lacked the club found on ankylosaurids.
facts.quote: La cola probablemente carecía del garrote que se encuentra en los anquilosaurios.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus lacked shoulder spikes, which were present in some other nodosaurids.
facts.quote: Los picos en el hombro, que presentaban algunos otros nodosáuridos, estaban ausentes.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus had particularly strong front legs with large muscle insertions, suggesting it may have been remarkably agile in life and capable of defensive charges like a modern rhinoceros.
facts.quote: Las patas delanteras eran particularmente fuertes, y tenían grandes inserciones para músculos grandes, que pueden sugerir que el animal habría sido asombrosamente ágil en vida, posiblemente pudiendo hacer cargas de la defensiva como un moderno rinoceronte.

facts.statement: The first Panoplosaurus fossil was found in 1917 by Charles M. Sternberg at Quarry 8 near Little Sandhill Creek.
facts.quote: El primer fósil fue encontrado en 1917 por Charles M. Sternberg en Quarry 8, cerca de Little Sandhill Creek.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen CMN 2759 was discovered in the Dinosaur Park Formation, which dates to the late middle Campanian, 76 million years ago.
facts.quote: Este holotipo , CMN 2759, fue descubierto en la Formación Dinosaur Park que data del Campaniano medio tardío, hace 76 millones de años.

facts.statement: Two larger specimens, ROM 1215 and RTMP 83.25.2, were found later; they contained skulls and provided information about the shoulder girdle and forelimbs.

facts.statement: Specimens of Panoplosaurus have also been reported from the Aguja Formation.
facts.quote: También se han reportado especímenes de Panoplosaurus de la Formación Aguja.

facts.statement: Panoplosaurus belonged to the family Nodosauridae within the infraorder Ankylosauria of the Thyreophora.
facts.quote: Panoplosaurus perteneció a la familia Nodosauridae dentro del infraorden Ankylosauria de los Thyreophora.

facts.statement: Originally assigned to Ankylosauridae, Panoplosaurus is now considered a member of Nodosauridae and a close relative of Edmontonia from the same formation.

facts.statement: In 1971, Walter Coombs referred the species of Edmontonia to a subgenus within Panoplosaurus, creating Panoplosaurus (Edmontonia) longiceps and Panoplosaurus (Edmontonia) rugosidens, but this has not found lasting acceptance.
